newsitem.title: CANADA: Bass deal may hasten MacMillan restructure.
newsitem.headline: Bass deal may hasten MacMillan restructure.

text.p: A move by the billionaire Bass brothers of Texas to invest in Canada's MacMillan Bloedel Ltd will likely increase pressure on the laggard forestry company to restructure, analysts said on Monday.

A group including the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan Board and Taylor and Co announced earlier they acquired a 9.5 percent stake in MacMillan. Taylor is the investment arm of the secretive Bass family in Fort Worth, Texas.
The group said the shares were acquired for investment purposes, and officials were not available for further comment.

Several analysts said the move might hasten a long-rumored restructuring at MacMillan that could include the sale of assets, notably its paper division and perhaps the spin-off of private timberlands.

"The situation is ripe...for investors willing to play the break-up game," said Salman Partners analyst Sam Magid. "This is a really good hunch on the part of the Bass family. The timing is perfect for this (restructuring) to crystallize."

MacMillan said the share purchase probably made the group its single biggest shareholder. A spokeswoman said the company had met with the investors and discussed corporate strategy. She described their stance as supportive.

MacMillan, Canada's biggest forestry concern, recently grouped its paper operations into a stand-alone division. The spokeswoman said the move was to enable the unit to focus more closely on its bottom line and was "not necessarily" a prelude to divestiture.

MacMillan has said for nearly a year that it is reviewing a gamut of options including sale of assets, acquisitions, financial restructuring and other moves. The spokeswoman said that process was continuing.
Earnings disappointments and lagging performance have hit its stock price.
One Wall Street analyst said earnings weakness was likely to continue in 1997 and it may be some time before the company is able to unlock value from its assets.

"They have talked a lot about selling their paper business. They are unhappy with it, but the question it comes down to is can they get an offer that makes sense," he said. "I would be surprised if they got a good price.
Potential buyers are hestitant to invest in MacMillan's home province of British Columbia because its regulatory and investment climate is perceived to be hostile to the industry, he said.
But he said the Bass share purchase may well be a savvy long-term investment because MacMillan is "an undervalued large company with a great (wood) fiber base."

Two of the four Bass brothers, Sid Richardson Bass and Lee Marshall Bass, have amassed a fortune built upon family oil holdings and command a reputation as shrewd and bold investors. They have invested previously in Marathon Oil and Texaco Inc and are perhaps best known for taking a big stake in Walt Disney Co.
One Wall Street source said the pair were likely to keep a low profile at MacMillan. "They are very quiet and don't like publicity," he said. "They are very hard to follow."
